questions.q: What is the key difference between a validation gate and an approval gate?
options: They are the same thing with different names
A validation gate is an automated, threshold-based check, while an approval gate pauses the pipeline for an explicit human decision on something that doesn't reduce to a number
Approval gates only exist in GitLab, never GitHub Actions
A validation gate always requires a human reviewer
questions.explain: Validation gates automate yes/no checks against metrics; approval gates are reserved for judgment calls that a threshold can't capture.

questions.q: In GitHub Actions, what actually enforces the pause on a job using a `production` environment with required reviewers?
options: The `kubectl apply` command itself
The environment's protection rules configured in the repository settings, not anything written directly in the job's YAML steps
A cron schedule
The order of jobs in the workflow file
questions.explain: The pause comes from the GitHub environment's configured protection rules (required reviewers), which the job references via the `environment` key.

questions.q: What does `when: manual` do in a GitLab CI job?
options: It automatically runs the job every hour
It leaves the job idle in the pipeline until someone with the right permissions manually triggers it
It deletes the job from the pipeline
It forces the job to run before all other jobs
questions.explain: when: manual marks a job as requiring an explicit trigger by a permitted user rather than running automatically.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue against putting an approval gate in front of every 5% canary step or every shadow deployment?
options: Because GitLab and GitHub Actions do not support it technically
Because those steps are low-risk by design, and gating them slows down the exact feedback loop canary and shadow exist to provide
Because canaries cannot be paused once started
Because approval gates only work on production environments
questions.explain: Canary and shadow deployments are deliberately low-risk; adding an approval gate to every incremental step defeats their purpose of fast, low-risk iteration.

questions.q: What information should a well-designed approval gate surface to the reviewer, according to the lesson?
options: Nothing — a bare approve/reject button is sufficient
Validation metrics for the candidate, canary/shadow results if available, and a diff of what changed and why
Only the name of the engineer who wrote the code
The full training dataset
questions.explain: Surfacing metrics, prior live-traffic results, and a change diff lets the reviewer make an informed decision quickly instead of having to dig for context.
